Backpropagation computes the gradient of any network, but for a long time, networks with more than a few layers did not train well. Adding layers did not improve the results, and larger networks became unstable. This section explains why and describes the techniques that solved the problem: activation functions that keep gradients alive, an initialization that keeps signals at a stable scale, normalization layers, regularization against overfitting, and optimizers that adapt their step sizes. Together, they turned neural networks into deep learning.

During training, the layer also keeps running averages of the means and variances; at inference, it uses these averages, so that the output for an example does not depend on the other examples in its batch. Batch normalization needs mini-batches large enough for reliable estimates, which is difficult for tasks with high-resolution inputs such as object detection, where only a few images fit into memory at once.

computes the mean and the variance over the features of a single example instead of over the batch. It needs no batch statistics, behaves identically in training and inference, and works for sequences of any length. Transformers and recurrent networks use it.
divides the features into groups and normalizes each group separately, a middle ground that works well for convolutional networks with small batches.

normalizes the weights of each layer instead of the activations and is often combined with group normalization. In practice, convolutional networks for image classification mostly use batch normalization, and transformers layer normalization.
A deep network with millions of parameters can memorize its training data, the overfitting of

shows the typical signs on a validation set: an almost perfect training accuracy, a much lower validation accuracy, and a gap that grows during training, sometimes with a phase in which the validation accuracy falls again. With regularization, a gap remains, but the validation accuracy follows the training accuracy much more closely. Making the network smaller is rarely the best remedy, because small networks cannot learn complex tasks. Regularization keeps the large network and constrains how it learns.

creates new examples from existing ones without new labels: for images, small rotations and crops, changes of brightness, added noise, or blur. The augmented examples also make the model robust against these small changes. Language models obtain their data through self-supervised learning, described in

: they learn to predict masked or next tokens in text collections of trillions of tokens. For a fixed computing budget, Hoffmann and colleagues found that a language model is best trained on about 20 tokens per parameter, so a model with one billion parameters needs about 20 billion tokens. A pretrained model can then be fine-tuned for a task with much less labeled data.
